Activation checkpointing trades recomputation cost for memory savings by discarding intermediate activations during the forward pass and recomputing them during backpropagation, but the granularity at which you draw checkpoint boundaries — per-layer, per-block, per-stage — determines how much memory you save versus how much recomputation latency you pay. In heterogeneous pipeline parallelism, stages differ in layer count, parameter density, and activation size, so a uniform checkpointing granularity that fits the memory budget of the heaviest stage over-checkpoints lighter stages (wasting recomputation budget) while a granularity tuned to lighter stages may leave the heaviest stage OOM. The expert worry that beginners entirely miss is recomputation overlap asymmetry: in a well-tuned pipeline, recomputation during the backward pass should overlap with bubble time or communication, but when a heavy stage's recomputation window is wider than the pipeline bubble it inhabits, it serializes with upstream backward passes and creates a throughput-collapsing cascade — each micro-batch's backward is delayed, widening the bubble for the next, compounding across gradient accumulation steps. A second expert concern is that recomputation itself is not compute-neutral: operations like attention (O(n²) in sequence length) cost dramatically more to recompute than to store, so checkpoint boundaries placed naively at transformer block edges can cause recomputation spikes precisely at the highest-FLOP operations. The interaction of these two effects — stage-heterogeneous memory pressure driving non-uniform checkpoint placement, which then produces uneven recomputation costs that misalign with pipeline scheduling — is what makes this a systems-level problem rather than a simple memory optimization.

In GPipe-style and 1F1B schedules (Narayanan et al., 2019; 2021), pipeline stages execute in a strict dependency order: stage k's backward pass cannot begin until stage k+1 has produced its gradient signal, so if stage k+1's recomputation overflows its bubble and delays its backward output, stage k stalls waiting — this is a hard sequential dependency, not a soft scheduling preference. The delay then propagates leftward through the pipeline: each upstream stage inherits the full overflow duration as added idle time, because there is no work-stealing or out-of-order execution available within a single micro-batch's backward chain. Gradient accumulation compounds this because the 1F1B schedule's key efficiency property — that micro-batch m+1's forward pass overlaps with micro-batch m's backward pass — breaks down when backward passes are stretched: the stage scheduler now finds a backward occupying the slot reserved for the next forward, forcing the forward to queue, which pushes the next backward's start time out by a full overflow duration. This cascades multiplicatively: with k gradient accumulation steps, a single-stage overflow of Δt can inflate total pipeline time by up to k·Δt in the worst case, because each accumulation step inherits the delay and the overlapping forward-backward interleave never recovers its phase alignment. Megatron-LM's interleaved 1F1B schedule (virtual pipeline stages, Narayanan et al., 2021) partially mitigates this by reducing bubble fraction from O(p/m) to O(p/vm) where v is the number of virtual stages, but recomputation overflow still serializes within each virtual stage's backward slot and can re-introduce effective bubble inflation if v is not tuned to recomputation cost. Empirically, PipeSwitch and similar systems report that even 15–20% recomputation overruns on a single heavy stage can degrade end-to-end throughput by 30–40% under aggressive gradient accumulation, because the phase misalignment persists for the entire accumulation window before a pipeline flush can resync.

The canonical strategy is selective checkpointing at sub-layer granularity: checkpoint after the QK softmax but before the AV matmul, preserving the attention weight matrix (O(n²) in memory) so that the backward pass need only recompute the cheap linear projections rather than the full O(n²) attention kernel — this is precisely the approach FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2023) exploits by storing only the softmax normalizer (a scalar per head per token, O(n)) and recomputing attention on-chip from Q, K, V in tiled SRAM passes, bounding recomputation to a single fused kernel rather than a full O(n²) materialization. A more aggressive bounding strategy is to treat each attention head's computation as an independent checkpoint unit: if a stage has h heads and recomputation of all h heads would overflow the bubble by Δt, you checkpoint at h/2 granularity, storing partial attention outputs for half the heads and recomputing only the other half — this halves recomputation time at the cost of O(n·h/2·d_head) additional activation memory per layer. The hidden cost is inter-stage activation buffer pressure: when the attention-heavy stage retains more partial activations (the stored softmax statistics or partial head outputs), these tensors must remain live in GPU memory until the backward pass consumes them, and in a pipelined system the backward pass arrives many micro-batches later — during the 1F1B steady state, the activation buffer for p-1 in-flight micro-batches accumulates simultaneously, so saving O(n) per layer per micro-batch scales to O(n·p·L) across p pipeline stages and L layers, which can dominate the memory budget of adjacent stages that were not themselves memory-constrained. Concretely, Megatron-LM's selective recomputation experiments (Korthikanti et al., 2022) showed that selectively checkpointing only attention (not MLP) reduced recomputation FLOP overhead from ~34% to ~8% of total training compute while keeping memory within budget on A100-80GB — but this relied on MLP activations being cheap to store relative to attention, an assumption that breaks when sequence lengths exceed ~4K tokens and attention's O(n²) storage again dominates. The practical resolution is adaptive granularity scheduling: profile recomputation cost per sub-layer at the target sequence length, compute the maximum recomputable FLOP budget that fits within the bubble slot, and greedily assign checkpoints from cheapest-to-recompute sub-layers first — but this requires per-stage profiling infrastructure that most frameworks (including stock PyTorch's checkpoint_sequential) do not provide natively, pushing the burden onto the practitioner.

Under full recomputation, the activation memory per stage per micro-batch is O(L_s · b · n · d) where L_s is layers per stage, b is micro-batch size, n is sequence length, and d is hidden dimension — only the checkpoint boundary tensors (inputs to each checkpointed block) are retained, and with p-1 in-flight micro-batches the total activation buffer is (p-1)·L_s·b·n·d. Under selective checkpointing that retains attention softmax statistics plus partial head outputs, the per-micro-batch retention grows to O(L_s · b · n · h) for the softmax normalizers plus O(L_s · b · n · h · d_head) for any retained partial attention outputs — at standard dimensions (h=32, d_head=128, d=4096) the retained-attention term is actually comparable to the full activation, so the crossover condition reduces to whether (p-1) · ΔM_retained > M_recomputed_saved, where ΔM_retained is the extra memory selective checkpointing keeps versus full recomputation. Plugging in Megatron-LM's 530B model configuration (p=35 pipeline stages, n=2048, d=20480, h=128) from Smith et al. (2022), selective checkpointing retains roughly 2.3× more activation memory per micro-batch than full recomputation at that stage depth, meaning the crossover had already occurred at p≈16 for that model's sequence length — beyond which selective checkpointing is strictly worse on memory despite being better on compute. The crossover pipeline depth scales as p_cross ∝ d/(n·h_retained) — deeper models with smaller per-stage layer counts push p_cross higher because L_s shrinks and reduces the retained buffer, but longer sequences drive n upward and collapse p_cross rapidly, which is why selective checkpointing configurations tuned for n=2048 break down at n=8192 even with identical pipeline depth. The practical implication is that checkpoint granularity should be a decreasing function of pipeline depth: at low p (≤8), retain aggressively (selective attention checkpointing) to save recomputation FLOP; at high p (≥16), revert toward full recomputation per block to avoid activation buffer explosion, accepting the recomputation overhead because the per-stage layer count L_s is small enough that full recomputation cost per stage is modest anyway.

The most principled scheduling modification is recomputation prefetching: rather than triggering recomputation at the moment the backward pass demands activations, the scheduler speculatively begins recomputing the next micro-batch's discarded activations during the idle slots of the current micro-batch's backward pass — this is the core idea behind Zero-Bubble Pipeline Parallelism (Qi et al., 2023), which classifies work into F (forward), B (full backward), and W (weight gradient) passes and reorders W passes to fill slots that would otherwise be bubbles, with recomputation slotted analogously into identified idle periods. A second approach is asynchronous recomputation via a dedicated recomputation stream: on CUDA devices with sufficient SM headroom, recomputation kernels can be dispatched on a secondary stream at lower priority while the primary stream executes communication and optimizer operations, so that recomputation runs in the background during all-reduce or P2P send/recv latency — NVIDIA's experiments with overlapping recomputation and pipeline communication in Megatron-LM showed 8–12% throughput recovery on A100 clusters with NVLink, though this requires careful stream synchronization to avoid race conditions on the activation buffer. A third modification is micro-batch reordering with recomputation slack injection: instead of strict FIFO ordering of micro-batches through the pipeline, the scheduler identifies micro-batches whose backward pass is not yet on the critical path and delays their backward dispatch by exactly Δt_recompute, creating a deliberate slack window during which the heavy stage completes recomputation without serializing with any upstream backward — this is analogous to the "1F1B-R" variant explored in PipeDream-Flush (Narayanan et al., 2021) where flush synchronization points are repositioned to absorb stragglers. The hidden constraint on all three approaches is activation buffer lifetime extension: prefetching recomputation earlier means the recomputed activations must be held in memory longer before the backward consumes them, and in a 35-stage pipeline this can add 2–4 micro-batches' worth of activation memory to the peak footprint, potentially negating the memory savings that motivated coarsening checkpoint granularity in the first place. Concretely, Zero-Bubble PP (Qi et al., 2023) demonstrated near-zero bubble fraction on GPT-style models at p=8 with this W-pass reordering approach, reducing bubble overhead from 12.5% (standard 1F1B) to under 1%, but reported that recomputation-heavy configurations required an additional 18% activation memory overhead to hold prefetched tensors — confirming that scheduling and memory budget are not independently optimizable and must be co-designed.

The primary hardware mechanism is CUDA Multi-Process Service (MPS) combined with SM partition capping via CUDA_MPS_ACTIVE_THREAD_PERCENTAGE: by launching the recomputation stream as a lower-priority MPS client capped at 30–40% of SMs, you statically reserve the remaining 60–70% for communication kernels (NCCL P2P sends/recvs and all-reduces), preventing recomputation from saturating the SM array during latency-critical pipeline boundary transfers — on A100 with 108 SMs, this translates to roughly 32–43 SMs for recomputation and 65–76 for communication, which matches NCCL's internal tuning heuristics for ring-allreduce on NVLink where it targets ~64 SM utilization for peak bandwidth. The condition under which SM partitioning becomes the binding throughput constraint is when the recomputation FLOP requirement exceeds what the capped SM partition can complete within the available slack window: if attention recomputation at sequence length n=8192 on a 30%-capped partition requires 2.4ms but the pipeline bubble slot is only 1.8ms, the recomputation spills past the window and the main stream must stall waiting for activations — at this point you have both degraded communication throughput (from the partition cap) and recomputation overflow, strictly worse than either naive approach alone. The fundamental tension is that communication kernels and recomputation kernels have opposing SM efficiency curves: NCCL benefits from fewer, fully-occupied SMs running at peak memory bandwidth, while recomputation GEMMs need broad SM coverage for compute throughput — any static partition satisfies one at the expense of the other, which is why dynamic SM reconfiguration (not yet exposed in production CUDA) remains an open hardware-software co-design problem.
